title: Job 27:13–23
context: In the book as it stands, Job is still speaking (27:1, 11–12), and these verses describe “the portion of a wicked man with God” (27:13): children given to the sword, widows without lament, wealth handed to the just, a flimsy house, and sudden ruin carried off by terrors, storm, and the east wind (27:14–23). The opening line closely resembles Zophar’s summary in 20:29, and the passage sounds much like the friends’ own teaching on the fate of the wicked. Because the third cycle contains no speech from Zophar, some readers propose that 27:13–23 is Zophar’s missing third speech, or part of it. Others keep Job as the speaker and read the passage in one of several ways: as Job turning the friends’ doctrine back on them as a warning, since he has just called them “altogether vain” (27:12) and wished his enemy to be as the wicked (27:7); as Job affirming that God does finally judge the wicked while still denying that this explains his own suffering; or as Job quoting the friends’ position in order to answer it. These notes present the text as it stands, with Job speaking, alongside the proposed reassignment, without deciding between them. Whoever speaks, the passage voices the friends’ familiar theme, which the book does not adopt as a full account of suffering; the LORD’s later verdict that the friends have not spoken of him what is right (42:7) does its own work. Both Arminian and Reformed readers affirm that God will judge wickedness, and both decline to read the passage as a rule that every sufferer is wicked.

verses.text: “This is the portion of a wicked man with God, the heritage of oppressors, which they receive from the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: The passage opens with “the portion of a wicked man with God,” closely echoing Zophar in 20:29. Some readers therefore assign these verses to Zophar, while the text as it stands keeps Job speaking. Arminian readers note that either way the verse states a real biblical truth, that God judges oppressors, without proving that Job is one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm God’s final justice toward the wicked and note that Job himself never denies it, only its mechanical application to his case (compare 21:7–15). They hold the attribution question open. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a statement about God’s justice that cannot be turned into a verdict on Job.

verses.text: If his children are multiplied, it is for the sword. His offspring will not be satisfied with bread.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says that if the wicked man’s children multiply, it is for the sword, and his offspring will not be satisfied with bread. Arminian readers note how this echoes the friends’ earlier speeches (compare 5:4; 20:10), and they hear it painfully against Job’s own loss of his children (1:18–19), which the reader knows was not punishment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse describes judgment on the wicked as reaching their household, a theme found elsewhere in Scripture, yet they caution against reading every family tragedy as divine retribution, since the prologue shows otherwise for Job. Shared ground: both traditions hear the verse as a general warning, not a key to Job’s losses.

verses.text: Those who remain of him will be buried in death. His widows will make no lamentation.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says those who remain of the wicked will be buried in death and his widows will make no lamentation. Some readers take “death” here as a reference to plague or pestilence, though this is uncertain. Arminian readers hear a grim picture of a life that leaves no one grieving, and they see a warning about the emptiness of wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the absence of mourning as a sign that the wicked man’s life brought no lasting blessing, a fitting end to oppression in this poetic picture. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry about the end of the oppressor, and both hold the attribution of the passage and the precise sense of “death” with care.

verses.text: Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare clothing as the clay;
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker pictures the wicked heaping up silver as the dust and preparing clothing as the clay. Arminian readers see the image of vast wealth gathered by oppression, and they connect it with Jesus’ warnings about storing up treasure on earth (compare Matthew 6:19), noting that what is hoarded unjustly cannot be kept.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse as describing the futility of wealth gained apart from God, a theme taken up in Ecclesiastes and the Psalms (compare Psalm 49:16–17). Shared ground: both traditions agree that riches cannot secure a person before God, and both read the verse as a general truth rather than a description of Job, who was rich and righteous.

verses.text: he may prepare it, but the just will put it on, and the innocent will divide the silver.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says the wicked may prepare it, but the just will put on the clothing and the innocent will divide the silver. Arminian readers hear a reversal in which God’s justice transfers the oppressor’s gains to the righteous (compare Proverbs 13:22), and they see hope for the poor who have been wronged.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence overruling the plans of the wicked, so that their gains serve the righteous in the end. They note that Job’s own restoration (42:10) comes from God’s grace rather than from a fixed rule. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confidence in God’s ultimate justice, without making it a timetable for every case.

verses.text: He builds his house as the moth, as a booth which the watchman makes.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says the wicked man builds his house as the moth, as a booth a watchman makes. Many readers take both images as pictures of something flimsy and temporary, though what exactly the moth image refers to is debated. Arminian readers hear a warning that a life built on injustice has no lasting foundation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers connect the image with Jesus’ parable of the house built on sand (Matthew 7:26–27), and they see the folly of security apart from God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of fragile security, while holding the precise sense of the moth image with care and leaving the attribution of the passage open.

verses.text: He lies down rich, but he will not do so again. He opens his eyes, and he is not.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says the wicked man lies down rich but will not do so again; he opens his eyes and is gone. Arminian readers hear the suddenness of judgment and the uncertainty of riches, and they connect it with Jesus’ parable of the rich fool, whose soul was required of him in a single night (compare Luke 12:20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sudden loss as God’s judgment overtaking the secure, a common biblical theme (compare Psalm 73:18–19). They note that Psalm 73 also wrestles honestly with the prosperity of the wicked, much as Job does in chapter 21. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning about false security, not a rule for timing.

verses.text: Terrors overtake him like waters. A storm steals him away in the night.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says terrors overtake the wicked man like waters and a storm steals him away in the night. Arminian readers hear the friends’ familiar picture of terror chasing the wicked (compare 18:11), and they note that Job himself has known terror without being wicked (3:25), which shows the limits of this picture as a diagnosis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sudden terror as a poetic image of God’s judgment overtaking those who defy him, and they affirm that God does judge wickedness in his time. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning about judgment, while recognizing from the book’s wider story that terror and calamity do not by themselves prove a person wicked.

verses.text: The east wind carries him away, and he departs. It sweeps him out of his place.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says the east wind carries the wicked man away and sweeps him out of his place. The east wind is commonly understood as a scorching desert wind, used in Scripture as an image of sudden destruction (compare 15:2; Hosea 13:15). Arminian readers see a vivid picture of how quickly unjust security can vanish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the wind in Scripture is under God’s command (compare Psalm 148:8), so the image portrays God’s judgment working through creation. They hold the meteorological detail loosely. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry about sudden judgment, not as a claim that every storm is aimed at the wicked.

verses.text: For it hurls at him, and does not spare, as he flees away from his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker says it hurls at the wicked man without sparing as he flees from its hand. Whether “it” and “his hand” refer to the wind, to God, or to both is not entirely clear, and readers differ. Arminian readers hear the hopelessness of trying to escape judgment once one has persisted in wickedness and refused God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as God’s judgment, which no one can outrun (compare Amos 9:2–3), whatever the precise referent of the pronouns. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that judgment cannot be escaped by flight, and both hold the grammar and the attribution of the passage open rather than forcing a single answer.

verses.text: Men will clap their hands at him, and will hiss him out of his place.
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker closes with people clapping their hands at the wicked man and hissing him out of his place, gestures of scorn (compare Lamentations 2:15). Arminian readers hear the end of the oppressor’s honor, and they note how ironic this picture is for Job, who has himself become an object of mockery (30:1, 9) without being wicked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the public scorn as part of the poetic picture of the wicked man’s downfall, and they note that the book will soon show Job, not the friends, restored and vindicated (42:10). Shared ground: both traditions read the closing line as the end of a warning about judgment, whose speaker the book leaves for readers to weigh.
